q: In an orchestrator-worker architecture, what is the orchestrator's primary responsibility?
o: Run every tool call itself so the workers can stay stateless
Decompose the task, delegate subtasks to workers, and synthesize their results
Fine-tune each worker model on the task data
Approve every worker output manually before it is produced
e: The orchestrator plans and splits the work, dispatches it to workers, then combines their outputs. Workers handle narrow subtasks with their own focused context.

q: Which pattern has one model call produce a draft, a second call critique it against explicit criteria, and the critique feed back into a revision?
o: Routing
Evaluator-optimizer
Sectioning (parallelization)
Prompt caching
e: Evaluator-optimizer is an iterative generate-and-critique loop. It works best when there are clear evaluation criteria and refinement measurably improves the result.

q: A support system classifies each incoming message as billing, technical, or refund and sends it to a specialised prompt for that category. Which pattern is this?
o: Prompt chaining
Evaluator-optimizer
Routing
Fan-out / fan-in
e: Routing classifies the input first and directs it to a specialised downstream handler, so each prompt can be optimised for its own category.

q: A long-running agent is approaching its context limit mid-task. Which strategy best preserves continuity?
o: Drop the system prompt to free space
Summarise older turns into a compact record of decisions, state and open items, then continue with recent turns
Restart from scratch with no history
Delete tool results at random
e: Compaction keeps what matters (goals, decisions, current state, unfinished work) while freeing space. Discarding the system prompt or history at random loses essential information.

q: Where should an agent keep facts it needs to remember across separate sessions?
o: In the model itself, because the API remembers prior sessions automatically
In an external store such as files or a database that is read back into context when needed
In a larger max_tokens value
In the tool_choice parameter
e: The API is stateless and the model does not learn from your calls, so durable memory must live outside the model and be loaded into context when relevant.

q: What is the main benefit of having an agent write an explicit plan before it starts calling tools on a complex task?
o: It guarantees the final answer is correct
It makes the approach reviewable and reduces wandering and rework, since the plan can be checked and revised
It removes the need for any tools
It makes input tokens free
e: A plan exposes the intended approach early, so you or the agent can catch mistakes cheaply. It does not guarantee correctness.

q: Which termination design is most robust for an autonomous coding agent?
o: Always stop after exactly three turns
Stop when a verifiable success check passes (for example, the tests), with iteration and budget limits as backstops
Stop when the model says it feels confident
Never stop until a user interrupts
e: Verifiable success criteria give an objective finish line. Hard limits on iterations, time and cost prevent runaway runs if that criterion is never met.

q: Claude returns the response below. How should you send the tool results back?
o: Two separate user messages, one per result
One user message containing two tool_result blocks, each with the matching tool_use_id
Only the first result, since the second is redundant
An assistant message containing two tool_result blocks
e: All results for parallel tool calls go back together in a single user message, one tool_result per tool_use_id.

q: In a prompt chain (outline, then draft, then polish), what is a 'gate' between steps?
o: A rate limiter on API calls
A programmatic check on the intermediate output that must pass before the next step runs
A second model that rewrites the prompt
A cache breakpoint
e: Gates validate intermediate results (format, length, required content) so errors are caught early instead of propagating down the chain.

q: When is a fixed workflow usually a better choice than an autonomous agent?
o: When the steps are not known in advance
When the steps are predictable and well defined, so you want lower cost, lower latency and more consistent behaviour
When you need the model to choose its own tools every time
Never; agents are always preferable
e: Agents trade cost and latency for flexibility. If the path is known up front, a workflow is simpler, cheaper, faster and easier to test.

q: An agent executes Python code that the model generated. Which safeguard is most appropriate?
o: Run it as root so permission errors never occur
Run it in an isolated sandbox with restricted filesystem, network and resource limits
Run it directly on the production host but log the output
Trust it, since the model is aligned
e: Model-generated code is untrusted. Isolation and least privilege limit the damage from bugs, mistakes or injected instructions.

q: Why should a production agent log each model call and tool call under a shared run or trace ID?
o: It reduces token usage
It lets you reconstruct and debug a run, audit its actions, and measure cost and latency per step
It is required by the Messages API
It prevents prompt injection
e: Tracing makes agent behaviour observable. Without it, diagnosing a bad run across many steps is guesswork.

q: Which self-correction loop is most reliable for code generation?
o: Ask Claude to rate its own confidence from 1 to 10
Run the tests or linter and feed the actual failures back to Claude
Ask the same question again and take the first answer
Raise max_tokens
e: Concrete, verifiable feedback (test failures, compiler errors) grounds revisions in reality. Self-reported confidence is not a reliable signal.

q: What is a key trade-off of using multiple cooperating agents instead of a single agent?
o: Multi-agent systems always use fewer tokens
Higher token usage and added coordination complexity, in exchange for parallelism and focused contexts
They remove the need for prompts
They cannot use tools
e: Multi-agent designs can speed up and organise broad tasks, but they multiply token use and make coordination, debugging and consistency harder.

q: A task will span many context windows. Which practice best lets a fresh context pick up where the last one stopped?
o: Keep a progress file (done, to-do, decisions) and commit work, and have each new context read it at the start
Repeat the entire previous transcript in every prompt
Rely on the model to remember the earlier session
Lower the temperature
e: Persistent artifacts such as a progress log and version-control history give each new context a compact, reliable picture of the state of the work.

q: Which approach best evaluates an agent's quality?
o: Count only the total tokens used
Measure end-to-end task success on a representative set and inspect trajectories (tool choices, errors, step counts)
Check only that the final answer is long
Test only on easy happy-path examples
e: Outcome metrics show whether the agent succeeds. Trajectory review shows why it fails and where it wastes steps.

q: Where should team-wide coding conventions for Claude Code live so they are shared through version control?
o: ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md in each developer's home directory
A CLAUDE.md file in the repository root that is committed
The .claude/settings.local.json file
An environment variable on each laptop
e: A committed project-level CLAUDE.md is loaded for everyone who works in the repo. A home-directory CLAUDE.md is personal and applies across projects.

q: Which Claude Code settings source has the highest precedence?
o: User settings (~/.claude/settings.json)
Shared project settings (.claude/settings.json)
Local project settings (.claude/settings.local.json)
Enterprise managed policy settings
e: Managed policy settings sit at the top and cannot be overridden by user or project settings. Below them come command-line arguments, then local project, shared project and user settings.

q: What is .claude/settings.local.json intended for?
o: Team-wide settings committed to the repo
Personal, project-specific overrides that are not committed to version control
Global defaults for all projects
Organisation-wide enforced policy
e: The local settings file holds your own per-project preferences and is normally git-ignored, so it is not shared with teammates.

q: Where do project-scoped custom slash commands live?
o: claude_desktop_config.json
Markdown files in .claude/commands/
The scripts section of package.json
The .mcp.json file
e: Each Markdown file in .claude/commands/ becomes a slash command named after the file, and committing the folder shares the commands with the team.

q: A subagent definition file in .claude/agents/ typically consists of what?
o: Only a JSON schema
YAML frontmatter (such as name, description and optional tools) followed by a system prompt in the Markdown body
A compiled binary
A Dockerfile
e: Subagents are Markdown files with frontmatter describing the agent and when to use it, followed by the instructions that act as its system prompt.

q: What does Plan Mode in Claude Code do?
o: Disables all tools permanently
Lets Claude explore the codebase read-only and propose a plan for your approval before making edits
Runs the whole task in the background without prompts
Automatically commits every change
e: Plan Mode separates investigation from execution, so you can review and adjust the approach before any files are changed.

q: What does the /compact command do?
o: Compresses the repository into an archive
Summarises the conversation so far to free up context while keeping the key information
Deletes all project files
Disables extended thinking
e: /compact replaces a long history with a summary, which helps long sessions stay within the context window. You can add instructions about what to preserve.

q: A PreToolUse hook script exits with code 2. What happens?
o: The tool call runs as normal
The tool call is blocked and the hook's stderr message is fed back to Claude
The whole Claude Code session is terminated
The hook result is ignored
e: Exit code 2 is a blocking error for PreToolUse hooks: the call does not run, and Claude sees the stderr text so it can adjust. Exit code 0 means success.

q: Given this hooks configuration, when does the hook run?
o: Before every Bash command
After Claude's Edit or Write tool calls complete
When the session ends
When the user submits a prompt
e: PostToolUse runs after a tool finishes, and the matcher limits it to the Edit and Write tools. That is a common way to run a formatter after file changes.

q: How can a CLAUDE.md pull in the contents of another file such as docs/architecture.md?
o: #include docs/architecture.md
@docs/architecture.md (an @-import)
import('docs/architecture.md')
It is not possible; the content must be pasted in
e: CLAUDE.md supports @path imports, which keep the main file short while still giving Claude the referenced content.

q: What does this command do?
code: claude mcp add --scope project my-server -- npx -y some-mcp-server
o: Installs the server for you only, in a private location
Records the server in a .mcp.json file in the project so teammates share it
Adds the server to your organisation's managed policy
Starts the server once and then removes it
e: Project scope writes to .mcp.json in the repository so the team uses the same MCP configuration. Local and user scopes are private to you.

q: What is the benefit of progressive disclosure in Agent Skills?
o: Every skill's full instructions are always loaded into context
Only each skill's short name and description are loaded up front; the full instructions and files load only when the skill is relevant
Skills are loaded only at the end of the session
Skills run without any instructions
e: Loading details on demand keeps context lean, so many skills can be available without paying their full token cost on every turn.

q: What makes few-shot examples most effective?
o: Many near-identical examples
Diverse, relevant examples that cover edge cases and match the desired output format
A single very long example
Examples in a different format from the desired output
e: Varied examples help Claude generalise the pattern, and examples that mirror the target format show exactly what you want. Identical ones can cause over-fitting to surface details.

q: For a multi-step reasoning problem, which technique typically improves accuracy when extended thinking is not used?
o: Ask for the final answer in a single word
Ask Claude to reason step by step, for example inside <thinking> tags, before giving the final answer
Set max_tokens very low
Remove all context from the prompt
e: Letting Claude work through intermediate steps before answering improves performance on complex tasks. Separating the reasoning from the final answer also makes the output easier to parse.

q: A prompt contains a very long document and a question about it. Where does Anthropic's guidance suggest putting the question?
o: Before the document only
After the document, at the end of the prompt
Hidden in the middle of the document
Placement makes no difference
e: Putting long documents first and the query last tends to improve response quality, especially with long inputs.

q: What does assigning a role in the system prompt, such as 'You are a senior security reviewer', primarily do?
o: Gives Claude new technical capabilities
Focuses Claude's tone, vocabulary and perspective on the domain
Increases the context window
Disables safety behaviour
e: A role steers style and focus. It does not add capabilities, so you still need to supply the facts and constraints the task requires.

q: You are classifying support tickets into fixed categories. Which setting is most appropriate for the temperature parameter?
code:
client.messages.create(
    model=MODEL,
    max_tokens=200,
    temperature=...,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Classify this ticket as billing, bug, or other: ..."}],
)
o: Close to 0.0, for consistent, deterministic-leaning output
1.0, for maximum creativity
A random value for each request
It has no effect on classification
e: Analytical and extraction tasks benefit from low temperature for consistency. Higher values suit brainstorming and creative writing.

q: Why break a complex task into a chain of smaller prompts?
o: Chaining is always cheaper and faster
Each step is simpler to get right, easier to debug, and can be validated independently
The API requires one task per call
It prevents hallucination entirely
e: Focused steps improve accuracy and make failures easy to localise. Chaining can cost more calls and latency, so use it when the quality gain is worth it.

q: Which instruction best reduces fabricated answers in document Q&A?
o: Always give a confident answer
Answer only from the provided document, and say 'I don't know' if the answer is not there
Never refuse any question
Increase the temperature
e: Giving Claude explicit permission to say it does not know, and restricting it to the supplied source, reduces invented details.

q: Before rolling out a prompt change to production, what should you do?
o: Ship it if the first example you try looks good
Run it against a representative evaluation set and compare it with the current baseline
Test only on the newest examples
Remove existing tests so they do not block you
e: A prompt change can fix one case while breaking others. A fixed eval set makes regressions visible.

q: Which phrasing is generally the most effective way to control formatting?
o: Don't use bullet points or headers.
Respond in flowing prose paragraphs.
Never ever use formatting!!!
Format it nicely.
e: Telling Claude what to do is clearer than only listing what not to do, and a specific description beats a vague or emphatic one.

q: What is the main purpose of the tags in this prompt?
code:
Summarise the contract below in three bullet points.

<contract>
{{CONTRACT_TEXT}}
</contract>
o: They are required syntax for the API
They clearly separate the document from the instructions and make the content easy to refer to
They encrypt the contract text
They reduce the token count
e: XML-style tags give structure that helps Claude tell data from instructions and lets you reference sections by name. They are a convention, not required syntax.

q: For Q&A over a long document, which technique improves faithfulness to the source?
o: Ask Claude to first extract the relevant quotes, then answer using only those quotes
Ask Claude to answer as fast as possible
Remove the document and rely on memory
Ask for the longest possible answer
e: Quote-first grounding focuses Claude on the actual evidence before it writes an answer, which reduces drift and unsupported claims.

q: What is the most reliable way to control response length?
o: Rely only on max_tokens
State explicit length and format expectations in the prompt (such as 'two sentences'), and use max_tokens only as a backstop
Ask for a 'short' answer without any detail
Set temperature to 0
e: max_tokens cuts output off rather than shaping it. Clear instructions let Claude write a complete answer of the right size.

q: In MCP, which primitive is primarily controlled by the model?
o: Resources
Prompts
Tools
Roots
e: Tools are model-controlled: Claude decides when to call them. Resources are application-controlled context, and prompts are user-invoked templates.

q: Which MCP transport is typically used for a local server launched by the client as a subprocess?
o: Streamable HTTP
stdio
gRPC
SMTP
e: stdio communicates over the subprocess's standard input and output. Streamable HTTP is used for remote servers.

q: In MCP architecture, what is the 'host'?
o: The server that exposes tools
The AI application (such as Claude Desktop or an IDE) that manages one or more MCP clients
The language model's weights
The OAuth provider
e: The host is the application the user interacts with. It creates a client for each server connection, and each client talks to one server.

q: You expose tools from several MCP servers. What helps Claude avoid mixing them up?
o: Give every tool the same short name
Use clear, specific, consistently namespaced names such as github_create_issue
Remove all descriptions
Use random identifiers for names
e: Distinct, descriptive names (and prefixes by service) reduce wrong-tool selection and name collisions.

q: A search tool returns 5,000 rows to Claude on every call. What is the best improvement?
o: Send all rows anyway; more data is always better
Add filtering, pagination and a concise response option so only relevant data is returned
Increase the temperature
Rename the tool
e: Large payloads waste context and bury the useful part. Return what is needed and let Claude request more if required.

q: Which tool-set design usually leads to better tool selection?
o: One tool with 40 optional parameters that does everything
A focused set of well-scoped tools with distinct purposes, merging overlapping ones
Hundreds of near-duplicate tools
Tools with identical descriptions
e: Clear, non-overlapping tools are easier for the model to choose between. Too many similar tools increases confusion and token use.

q: What message format does MCP use between clients and servers?
o: GraphQL
JSON-RPC 2.0
SOAP
Protocol Buffers only
e: MCP messages (requests, responses and notifications) use JSON-RPC 2.0 over the chosen transport.

q: This tool is served over the stdio transport. What is the problem with the print() call?
o: print is not allowed in Python 3
It writes to stdout, which carries the protocol messages, and can corrupt the stream; log to stderr instead
It makes the function return a string
There is no problem
e: With stdio, stdout is the protocol channel. Stray output breaks message framing, so send logs to stderr or use a logging library configured for stderr.

q: Why validate tool inputs on the server even if the tool has an input_schema?
o: Schemas are never used by Claude
The schema guides the model but does not guarantee safe input; model mistakes or untrusted content can still produce bad values, so enforce checks and authorization in code
Validation makes the tool faster
Validation is only needed for read-only tools
e: Treat tool arguments as untrusted input. Server-side validation and permission checks are your real security boundary.

q: Which tool output is easier for Claude to use correctly?
o: Only opaque UUIDs such as 7f3a9c1e-...
Human-readable names alongside IDs, such as 'Jane Smith (user_4821)'
Binary data
An empty string on success
e: Meaningful identifiers help the model reason about and report results accurately. Include IDs for follow-up calls, but pair them with readable context.

q: Remote MCP servers that need user authorisation typically rely on which standard?
o: OAuth-based authorisation (the MCP spec builds on OAuth 2.1)
A shared password sent in the URL query string
No authentication; remote servers are always public
Client certificates only, issued by Anthropic
e: Remote servers use OAuth flows so users can grant scoped access without sharing credentials. Never put secrets in URLs.

q: Why can adding more context to a prompt sometimes hurt response quality?
o: Longer prompts are always rejected
Irrelevant or distracting content dilutes the signal and can reduce accuracy, so curate what you include
The model cannot read more than 100 words
Context is ignored after the first line
e: More context is not automatically better. Include what is relevant, and trim or summarise the rest.

q: Which workload best fits the Message Batches API?
o: Real-time customer chat
Large, non-urgent bulk jobs such as classifying 100,000 documents overnight at lower cost
Interactive code autocomplete
Live voice conversations
e: Batches are asynchronous and discounted, with results typically available within a day, so they suit offline bulk processing rather than latency-sensitive use.

q: How can you estimate the input token count of a request before sending it?
o: Use the API's token counting endpoint
Assume characters divided by 4 is always exact
Assume tokens always equal words
It can only be known after billing
e: The token counting endpoint reports input tokens for a prospective request. Rules of thumb are only rough approximations.

q: In a RAG pipeline, retrieved chunks are often only loosely relevant. Which change most directly improves precision?
o: Pass all retrieved chunks, however many
Add a reranking step (along with better chunking or hybrid search) and send only the top chunks to Claude
Lower max_tokens
Remove the user's question from the prompt
e: Reranking re-scores candidates for relevance so Claude sees fewer, better passages, which reduces noise and cost.

q: Why use streaming for requests that generate very long outputs?
o: Streaming makes the model smarter
It helps avoid HTTP timeouts on long generations and shows partial output sooner
It is the only way to use tools
It reduces input tokens
e: Long non-streaming requests risk timeouts, and streaming gives users incremental feedback while the response is generated.

q: When using an LLM as a judge in automated evaluations, which step is important?
o: Use it with no rubric
Write a clear rubric and calibrate the judge against human-labelled examples
Trust the first score it gives
Use temperature 1.0 for variety
e: Judges can be biased or inconsistent. A rubric plus a human-labelled check set tells you whether its scores can be trusted.

q: What reliability pattern does this loop implement?
o: Routing
Bounded validate-and-retry with the error fed back to Claude
Prompt caching
Fan-out / fan-in
e: The output is validated, and on failure the specific error is sent back so Claude can correct it. The attempt limit keeps the loop bounded.

q: A tool that charges a customer's card might be retried after a network timeout. What prevents a double charge?
o: A lower temperature
An idempotency key, so repeated requests for the same operation are deduplicated
A larger max_tokens
Asking Claude to be careful
e: Idempotency keys make retries safe: the second attempt returns the first result instead of repeating the side effect.

q: During a prolonged API outage, which design best preserves the user experience?
o: Show a raw stack trace
Degrade gracefully: queue work, serve cached or limited functionality, and show a clear status message
Retry in a tight loop forever
Silently return empty answers
e: Plan fallbacks ahead of time. Users prefer clear communication and reduced functionality over errors or silent failures.
